quote: Dieser Ausdruck, selbst wenn nicht ein- facher, ist doch wahrscheinlich bequemer und auf beliebige [-Formen-] ternäre etc. Substitutionen verallgemeinerungs- fähig
english: This expression, even if not simpler, is nevertheless probably more convenient and generalizable to arbitrary ternary etc. substitutions.
topic: Notes on the eight types of singularities of space curves and their duality, expressing a symbol for the discriminant via differential operators, and reflections on how to approach difficult research problems.

triage.modern_statement: This is a remark about method, not a precise problem. Hilbert seems to have written a symbolic expression for the discriminant of a binary form using differential operators, something like Cayley's Omega process or polarization operators. He then guessed that this form, though not simpler, would be more convenient and would carry over from binary substitutions (SL2 acting on binary forms) to ternary and higher ones (SL3 and beyond acting on ternary and n-ary forms). In modern terms the question is whether a differential-operator formula for the discriminant of a binary form extends to discriminants or invariants of n-ary forms. The note does not say which expression he meant, so no single precise statement can be reconstructed.
triage.answered_by: No specific later answer can be identified. In general terms, differential-operator methods for invariants were extended past the binary case. The best-known example is Cayley's Omega process for SL_n, which Hilbert himself used in his finiteness work around 1890 and which was later generalized (e.g. Ferrer, Proc. AMS 2007). Hilbert's own published discriminant papers from this period are about binary forms and the discriminant surface. I found no source that discusses this particular diary expression or the guess that it generalizes.

evidence.claim: Around this time Hilbert published papers on discriminants of binary forms, e.g. 'Ueber binäre Formen mit vorgeschriebener Discriminante', Math. Ann. 31 (1888) 482–492.
Hilbert, 'Ueber die Singularitäten der Discriminantenfläche', Math. Ann. 30 (1887) 437–441. This is related to the page's topics of singularities and discriminants.
Classical invariant theory proves the Hilbert Basis Theorem using a particular differential operator, Cayley's Omega process, which works for general n-ary forms.
Constructions due to Cayley and Hilbert (the Omega process) were later axiomatized and generalized to arbitrary affine algebraic monoids (Ferrer, Proc. AMS 2007).

triage.why: The note is Hilbert's informal guess that some differential-operator expression for the discriminant would be handier and would extend to ternary and higher substitutions. The expression itself is not given in the excerpt, so the exact claim cannot be pinned down or checked against the literature. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. The broader idea that differential operators extend to n-ary invariants did come true (the Omega process for SL_n, Hilbert's 1890 work, and modern generalizations). But I found no source tying any of this to this diary entry.
